questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Photons needed per carbon fixed
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the photon cost of fixing a stated amount of carbon dioxide
questions.stem: The chef's recipe costing sheet for the winter lettuce line budgets 1.2 mol of carbon dioxide fixed per kilogram of salad. At the standard requirement of nine photons per carbon dioxide, how many moles of photons does that kilogram cost?

options.text: About 10.8 mol of photons, since each mole of carbon dioxide needs nine moles of photons
About 21.6 mol of photons, because every carbon dioxide takes two rounds of the cycle
options.misconception: counts two photons per carbon dioxide as the requirement

options.text: About 1.2 mol of photons, because one photon fixes one carbon dioxide molecule
options.misconception: assumes a one to one photon to carbon dioxide ratio

options.text: About 10.8 mol of photons, plus extra moles to cover ATP turnover in the kitchen
options.misconception: charges ATP turnover separately from the photon ratio

questions.explanation: Nine photons are needed for each mole of carbon dioxide fixed, so 1.2 mol of carbon dioxide costs 10.8 mol of photons. One photon per carbon dioxide would double-count energy already in the ratio.
questions.hint: Multiply the moles of carbon dioxide by nine photons each.

questions.topic: ATP and NADPH demand of the Calvin cycle
questions.learningObjective: State the ATP and NADPH cost of fixing carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle
questions.stem: The costing sheet lists two salad batches. Batch A was fixed at 0.30 mol of carbon dioxide and Batch B at 0.50 mol. Which line gives the ATP and NADPH each batch must draw from the light reactions?

options.misconception: swaps the ATP and NADPH demand of the cycle

options.text: Batch A needs 0.90 mol ATP and 0.60 mol NADPH, and Batch B needs 1.50 and 1.00 mol
Batch A needs 0.30 mol ATP and 0.15 mol NADPH, and Batch B needs 0.50 and 0.25 mol
options.misconception: counts one turn of the cycle, not three per carbon dioxide

options.text: Batch A needs 1.80 mol ATP and 1.20 mol NADPH, and Batch B needs 3.00 and 2.00 mol
options.misconception: uses the glucose cost instead of the per-carbon cost

questions.explanation: One mole of carbon dioxide costs 3 mol ATP and 2 mol NADPH, so Batch A needs 0.90 mol ATP and 0.60 mol NADPH. Halving to one turn, or doubling to a glucose total, does not fit.
questions.hint: The cycle uses three ATP and two NADPH per carbon dioxide.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the exponential light attenuation model to a canopy
questions.stem: A sketch on the costing sheet shows a beam of light entering a canopy of leaf area index 4.0 with an attenuation coefficient of 0.45. What fraction of the beam is intercepted and what fraction reaches the floor?

options.misconception: treats light loss as linear in leaf area index

options.text: About 17% is intercepted and about 83% reaches the floor of the crop

options.text: About 83% is intercepted and about 17% reaches the floor of the crop
About 99% is intercepted and about 1% reaches the floor of the crop

questions.topic: Ion fluxes that open a stoma
questions.learningObjective: Identify the direction of proton pumping and ion movement in an opening stoma
questions.stem: A junior on the kitchen garden team wrote on the sheet: to open the stomata we pump protons into the guard cells, which pushes potassium in and makes the cells swell so the pore opens. Name the error.

options.text: Potassium leaves the guard cells during opening, and that loss is what makes the pore open
options.misconception: believes solute efflux is what opens the pore

options.text: Water leaves the guard cells during opening, so the cells swell and the pore opens
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the osmotic flow

options.text: Guard cells do not change shape during opening, since the pore widens on its own

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Stomatal pore area as a fraction of the leaf
questions.learningObjective: Design a measurement of the pore area fraction of a leaf
questions.stem: The kitchen garden wants to know what fraction of the leaf surface is actually pore, so the sheet records stomatal density and mean pore area for the salad cultivar. Design the measurement that gives this fraction.

answer.exemplar: Count stomata on a known area of epidermis, measure the length and width of each pore to obtain the mean pore area, then multiply density by mean pore area and divide by one million to express the result as a fraction of leaf area, repeating on several leaves and fields to average out local variation.

questions.explanation: The pore fraction is the number of stomata per unit area multiplied by the mean area of one pore, converted to a fraction. A sound design fixes a known sample area and repeats the count.
questions.hint: Multiply density by mean pore area, then convert units.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Stomatal density and its distribution
questions.learningObjective: Explain how stomatal density and size respond to bright dry habitats
questions.stem: Explain, for the costing sheet note, why leaves that grow in bright, dry conditions typically carry a higher density of smaller stomata than leaves from shaded, moist conditions.

answer.exemplar: Bright dry habitats lose water quickly, so selection favours many small pores: many small pores give as much total conductance as a few large ones while reducing the radius over which water vapour diffuses, so less water is lost for the same gas exchange. Shaded moist habitats can afford fewer, larger pores, which also intercept less light.

questions.explanation: The trade-off is between total pore area, which sets conductance, and pore radius, which sets how fast vapour escapes. Many small pores give the same conductance with less water loss.
questions.hint: Think about pore radius, not just total pore area.

questions.stem: On the sheet, lettuce stomatal conductance falls from 0.45 mol per square metre per second at 20 degrees Celsius to 0.225 mol per square metre per second at 28 degrees Celsius. Calculate the percentage fall in conductance.
questions.explanation: The fall is 0.225 mol per square metre per second, and dividing by the starting value of 0.45 gives a fall of one half, or 50%. Such a fall in a warm afternoon usually signals water stress.
questions.hint: Divide the fall by the starting value, then multiply by 100.

questions.topic: Stomatal pore area as a fraction of the leaf
questions.learningObjective: Design a comparison of water loss between high density and low density cultivars
questions.stem: Design a comparison, recorded on the recipe costing sheet, that tests whether a cultivar with high stomatal density but small pores loses water faster than one with low density and large pores.

answer.exemplar: Grow both cultivars at the same temperature, light and soil water, then place matched leaf sections on a balance or in a controlled-humidity chamber and record water loss per unit leaf area over one hour. Compare that rate with the product of stomatal density and mean pore area for each cultivar, expecting the many small pores to win on conductance.

questions.explanation: Water loss per unit leaf area depends on total pore perimeter as well as pore area, and many small pores offer more perimeter. Measure loss per unit area on matched leaves.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Stomatal density and its distribution
questions.learningObjective: Explain why stomata are concentrated on the lower leaf surface
questions.stem: In the costing sheet note, explain why the stomata of many crop leaves are concentrated on the lower surface rather than spread evenly over both surfaces.

answer.exemplar: On the lower surface the boundary layer of still, humid air is thicker, so water vapour diffuses away more slowly and the leaf loses less water than it would from the exposed upper surface. Concentrating stomata on the shaded, sheltered lower face therefore slows transpiration, and it keeps the light-facing surface free for photosynthesis.

questions.explanation: Stomatal density is a water-saving strategy, and the lower surface has a thicker layer of still, humid air. Spreading the same pores over the exposed upper surface raises water loss.
questions.hint: The lower surface has a thicker layer of still, humid air.

answer.exemplar: By midday the leaf to air vapour pressure difference is at its largest, so the potential water loss is greatest. answer.exemplar: The photon cost is set by the chemistry of the light reactions, not by the mass of the crop, so a cost per mole of carbon dioxide can be applied to any batch and compared between crops. questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: ATP and NADPH demand of the Calvin cycle
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the NADPH required for a stated carbon dioxide batch
questions.stem: The kitchen garden plans to fix 2.5 mol of carbon dioxide into triose phosphate in one run. How many moles of NADPH must the light reactions supply, at two moles of NADPH for every mole of carbon dioxide?
questions.explanation: Two moles of NADPH per mole of carbon dioxide gives 2.5 mol of carbon dioxide a requirement of 5.0 mol of NADPH. The ATP cost is separate, and the two should not be added when costing a batch.
questions.hint: Multiply the carbon dioxide by the NADPH cost per mole.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Leaf area index and light interception
questions.learningObjective: Calculate soil light in a canopy and judge the value of more leaves
questions.stem: Step one: the sheet gives a canopy leaf area index of 4.0 with an attenuation coefficient of 0.35 and an incident intensity of 1000 W per square metre. Step two: the head chef asks what intensity reaches the soil and whether more leaves would help.

options.text: About 753 W per square metre reaches the soil, so the canopy is still too sparse
options.misconception: subtracts the loss linearly instead of exponentially

options.text: About 247 W per square metre reaches the soil, and doubling the leaf area index doubles it
options.misconception: claims the light doubles when the leaf area index doubles

options.text: About 247 W per square metre reaches the soil, and more leaves would add little light
About 25 W per square metre reaches the soil, so the canopy must be thinned
options.misconception: reads the surviving fraction as a percent of the light

questions.explanation: The surviving fraction is the exponential of minus 1.4, about 0.247, so roughly 247 W per square metre reaches the soil. Since interception is nearly complete, more leaves would add little light.
questions.hint: Use the exponential of minus k times leaf area index.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ion fluxes that open a stoma
questions.learningObjective: Read two sets of guard cell fluxes from a diagram
questions.stem: One diagram on the sheet shows two sets of arrows around a guard cell. The first set has protons going out, then potassium going in, then water going in. The second set has potassium going out, then water going out, then the pore shut. What does the second set describe?

options.text: An opening sequence in which the pump first expels potassium and then draws in water
options.misconception: makes the outward potassium arrow part of opening

options.text: A neutral exchange in which potassium and water swap places without any turgor change
options.misconception: claims the exchange leaves turgor unchanged

options.text: A movement of protons only, since the ions and water do not move in the second set
options.misconception: ignores the ion and water arrows of the second set

options.text: The closure sequence, in which potassium and then water leave the guard cell

questions.explanation: The second set, with potassium and water leaving so that turgor falls and the pore shuts, is the closure sequence that abscisic acid triggers. The first set is the opening sequence.
questions.hint: Compare the direction of the ion arrows in the two sets.
